Patellar tendinopathy

One small randomized trial found greater improvement in function and quadriceps performance with laser plus eccentric exercise than with either treatment alone, while pain relief was not better than laser alone.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One small randomized trial found greater improvement in function and quadriceps performance with laser plus eccentric exercise than with either treatment alone, while pain relief was not better than laser alone.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tendons > Patellar tendinopathy category contains one unique publication, a randomized trial with 21 participants. There are no additional direct clinical studies, animal experiments, or in-vitro/ex-vivo records in the exact category.

Human and clinical evidence

Liu and colleagues randomized participants among laser treatment, eccentric exercise, and their combination. Each group contained seven people. The combined program improved pain, function, and quadriceps strength or endurance more than exercise alone on several outcomes. However, pain relief in the combined group was not significantly greater than laser alone, so the study does not show a clear added analgesic effect of combining the two approaches (Liu et al. 2014). The very small groups make the size and reliability of these differences uncertain.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified for patellar tendinopathy in the exact category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory or ex-vivo publication was identified for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial used an 810-nm near-infrared laser at 200 mW. Treatment was given three times weekly over four weeks, for 24 sessions, alongside a supervised eccentric exercise program in the combined group. The category does not contain a dose-comparison trial or a second protocol. These parameters should therefore be read as the schedule tested in one small study rather than as an established regimen.

Interpretation

The trial suggests a possible improvement in function and quadriceps performance when laser is paired with exercise, but it does not establish a reliable pain benefit or long-term tendon recovery.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for improved pain or function after PBM is added to eccentric exercise for patellar tendinopathy
Publications and records1 unique title in the exact category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The evidence consists of one randomized trial with 21 participants divided among three groups. The combined treatment improved several outcomes, but the sample was very small and pain relief did not differ between combined treatment and laser alone. Replication with an adequately powered trial and longer follow-up is needed.
